articles.text: A mistake has certainly been made in not holding a meeting of the Little Missouri Stockgrowers' association before the semi-annual meeting of the Montana association at Helena, which begins Aug. 25. The stockmen of the Little Missouri are almost all members of the Montana association, paying just as much in proportion toward the expenses of that association as the cowmen of Montana. For this, the only return they have received is the appointment of an inspector at Medora, and this was secured only after considerable wrangling. Nothing whatever could have been secured and nothing will be secured for Dakota cowmen except by authorized representatives of the Little Missouri association. If any of our cattlemen now go to Helena they will go simply as members of the Montana association, not authorized in any way to speak for Dakota. A moment's thought will show that this is all wrong. We should have authorized representatives ready and willing to demand what we need from the Montana association. The great difficulty our cowmen have to contend with is that we are considered a mere side issue by the Montana association, a good point from which to raise money but a poor one on which to spend it. For this reason our stockmen must be on the alert to gain all the advantage possible from the Montana association, and a lack of authorized representation is not the way to do this. It cannot be urged against a meeting of the Little Missouri association that it is too early. To send delegates from our association is a sufficient cause for calling a meeting, the cowmen at this time are not unusually busy and all arrangements could have been made a month ago for the beef round-up.
articles.summary: Editorial faults the failure to hold a Little Missouri Stockgrowers' association meeting to name delegates before the Montana association meeting at Helena on Aug. 25.

articles.text: The two best saddles and outfits on the river arrived Tuesday. One was for Theodore Roosevelt's own use and the other was a present by him to George Myers, a Chimney Butte cowboy. Silver conchas adorn the bits and spurs and on the latter are raised Maltese Cross and Elkhorn brands in solid gold. The outfits cost about $300 in Cheyenne.
articles.summary: Two fine saddles and outfits arrived Tuesday, one for Theodore Roosevelt and one his gift to Chimney Butte cowboy George Myers.

articles.text: Earl, infant son of J. D. Garver, died Sunday night of cholera infantum, after a sickness of only five or six hours. The funeral took place Monday afternoon from the home of the bereaved parents. Appropriate remarks were made by J. C. Fisher and T. W. Gordon, at the house and on Cemetery butte, where the burial took place. The parents wish to express their sincere thanks to all for their kindness during and after the funeral.
articles.summary: Earl, infant son of J. D. Garver, died of cholera infantum and was buried on Cemetery butte.

articles.text:
John Munro and Anne Brophy were married yesterday morning at the Catholic church, by Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan. The couple made a fine appearance and both looked their best. John and Annie are both general favorites here and the only possible objection to the union is that it did not occur some time ago. John Goodall and Mary Brophy were groomsman and bridesmaid
and they bore up well under the honors of the occasion. A tasty wedding-lunch was served at the Northern Pacific to all who called on the happy couple. Mr. and Mrs. Munro left on the evening train for Miles City on a bridal tour. They will return next Tuesday or Wednesday. A wedding ball is an event of the near future. The best wishes of the whole community follow the newly married couple and here's an old shoe from the Cow Boy for their future prosperity and happiness.
articles.summary: John Munro and Anne Brophy were married at the Catholic church by Father Martin of Mandan.

articles.text: A letter from Vic Smith, written at Billings, gives some further particulars relative to the hunting party. On the third day of the trip, Vic was prostrated with mountain fever and the same morning Mrs. DeMores and he killed four bear, she killing three, and Vic killing one near the camp-fire. Vic was sick five days and on the sixth, the Marquise and he went higher up into the mountains and killed a fine bear apiece, making six in all, besides which, William VanDriesche killed a handsome silver-tip. Elk, antelope and sheep were numerous. Brook trout was the staple food. The nights on the mountains were so cold that it was necessary to keep large log fires constantly burning. The Marquise was "loaded for bar" and would hunt nothing else. Seventeen were seen in all. Vic characterizes the Marquise as "an excellent shot and fearless as a cowboy." Miss Sophia, who accompanied the Marquise, comes in for a share of praise for her Tapley-like quality of being always pleasant under difficulties. The party finished their hunt by a 185-mile ride across the country in four days. Vic and Frank will be gone about a month longer, they having a good engagement meantime.
articles.summary: Vic Smith's letter from Billings describes the Marquise de Mores' bear hunt.

articles.headline: Cow Boy Dictionary.
articles.text:
Cow Boy Dictionary.

ADDENDA.

The following words were omitted from our dictionary. With these additions the list is about full. Should anyone know additional words we hope they will hand them in within a week, as by that time we wish to send the list to the revisors of Webster's Dictionary.

A

Aparajo, n. A pack-saddle, consisting of a leather pad stuffed with hay or hair, to which the load is strapped.

B

Bridle-trail, n. A trail used by horsemen. Usually too narrow or dangerous for a wagon.

Broncho-breaker, n. A man who makes a trade of breaking bronchos. Also called broncho-buster.

C

Cavia, n. A mare.

Cavio, n. A horse.

Chinook, n. A warm winter wind from the west. Originating from the Japan current and felt in the west and northwest, generally raising the temperature to forty or sixty degrees above zero.

F

Flying-brand, n. A brand made by flaring or curving the extremities of the letters or characters.

H

Hondou, n. The slip-knot to a lariat. Usually made with raw-hide or a mountain sheep's horn or it may be a knot in the rope itself.

Horn, n. The top part of the pommel.

J

Jerk-neck-team, n. A team hitched to the hind end of a lead wagon. The lead team has a driver but the jerk-neck does not.

L

Lazy-brand, n. A brand having the letter or character lying down.

Legaderos, n. The straps holding the stirrups.

M

Mess-wagon, n. The round-up wagon, carrying the food and cooking outfit.
articles.summary: Addenda to the Cow Boy's glossary of cowboy terms, to be sent to Webster's revisers.

articles.headline: A Specimen Oregon Girl.
articles.text:
A Specimen Oregon Girl.

The women, says a Portland, Oregon, correspondent, are very expert horsewoemn. The writer recently approached a mansion situated on Poverty Flat and observed the daughter of the house in the front yard cinching a man's saddle on an Oregon horse that objected to this proceeding. She was about the age where "standing with reluctant feet, womanhood and childhood meet." I offered my assistance as she was hopping around on her right foot, her left foot in the stirrup, while she firmly grasped the bridle-bit in the left hand.

The cayuse, meanwhile, was making mad bounds, bellowing as only an Oregon horse can bellow, and standing first on his hind feet and then on his head. "No, thanks;" "I can manage him!" she said, and vaulted into the saddle, [not?] sidewise, but otherwise.

The instant the girl gained the saddle and the horse felt that she was there, down went his head, an arch sprung in his back, and away he went, jumping stiff-legged, over sage brush six feet high, until horse and rider disappeared in the distance. After a while she came back at a thundering gallop, and reined up at the door a trifle excited, but smiling.

"You sit your horse like a Centaur. Where are you going, Miss Oregon?"

"Over to the Bully Creek Sunday School. You bet your life I can set him straight up, and don't you forget it."

Of course no corn fed girl in the State could hope to do so well as this product of the bunch hills. But character goes for more than trivial incident, and of the gentler sex it must be said that here, as elsewhere, they teach in the Sabbath schools and are the shining lights that point out the way onward and upward to the weary and faltering feet of the sons of men.
articles.summary: Reprinted anecdote from a Portland, Oregon correspondent about a girl breaking a bucking horse.

articles.headline: A Range Rider on the Calf Crop.
articles.text: Having been over a great deal of the cow country of southern Colorado in the saddle, this spring and summer, and having had similar trips for the last twenty-five years in Colorado in connection with the live-stock interests of the country, I can notice a big difference in the cattle breeding interests to what there was ten or fifteen years ago, and even five years ago. I have seen in different papers reports of the big calf crop, whereas my observation in the different round-ups and the different ranges I have been over, and the counts I have made of calves and of cows that were in calf and those that ought to have calves or be in calf, I say, Mr. Editor, that the calf crop is sadly short of what it should be and what it would be if the proper efforts were put forth by the owners and stock associations to remedy the causes responsible for this deficiency. The stock associations put me in mind of the old time peace commissioners that used to be sent out here to treat with the Indians. They would get the Indians together and have a big talk, and that ended the matter. The same is true with the associations; they know there is a deficiency, they know why they talk the matter over and perhaps they think will go right to work and remedy the evil, but they part and cool off, and time flies on, and before they realize it another year is gone and the same old complaint is more visible at the round-ups. The cow business as managed to-day is on the wane. The profits are less and the efforts put forth are less than they were years ago. One will see very few owners now with the round-ups, whereas years ago, the round-ups were composed principally of owners. They have dropped into the habit of sending out hired men and as few of them as possible. They gather up a bunch of cattle and drive them half a day; the calves all get back to the back end of the herd and seem thick and plenty, when if they would count the cows and heifers that comprise the bunch they would see those that had calves, those that were in calf and those that ought to have or be in calf; then the deficiency would be apparent, and would greatly modify the report of the calf crop. It is astonishing, really, the money that is being lost annually in Colorado in this one item of calves that are actually bred and what should be and might be bred if the proper efforts were put forth and the attention and appliances given to the business that should be. Men will keep an office in town and be there from early morn till late at night, knowing that to spend their time punching billiards will not pan out well in the fall, and put these same men into the cow business and they will seldom ever be seen in the saddle, and most of them will run the cow business on the plan the old woman did her hennery. Her theory was that the hens had to lay eggs any way and couldn't help themselves, but when she came to set eggs to raise broilers, she found herself left. Now I expect if this is published it will raise the ire of some; but pitch in, men, this thing needs stirring up. It took the shock of an earthquake to arouse old Rip Van Winkle; the breeders of cattle are asleep to their interests, and if it has to be an earthquake, let her come. I am ready.—[Cor. Colorado Live-Stock Review.
articles.summary: Reprinted letter from the Colorado Live-Stock Review arguing the calf crop is short through owners' neglect.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
Editor Cow Boy:—
I would like to ask through the columns of the Cow Boy, what has become of our Board of Health?

There are certain parties who would like to have the Board see that other people clean up their yards and remove all filth that would prove injurious, but not to trouble them about the filth in their own yards.

Last spring there was a man in town who kept hogs. The Marquis went to him and told him he must either kill or sell them. That man told me that he had to dispose of them at a sacrifice.

Now, Mr. Editor, I would like to ask if there were hogs kept all over town and around it, would the stench be one-half as bad as that which we get from the offal that is carried away from the slaughter-house and left uncovered to taint the air and breed a pestilence among our citizens? It certainly would not cost much to have that pile covered up and not compel us to breathe air that is rotten.

Something should also be done about draining off the water which has been standing so long between the hotel and saloon. It is breeding malaria that is felt by all in the vicinity.

A Citizen.
articles.summary: 'A Citizen' asks what has become of the Board of Health, complaining of slaughter-house offal and standing water.

articles.headline: A Bad Lands Excursion.
articles.text:
Mack. and Mack's. wife and Pack. and Pack's. wife have just returned from one and know all about it.

The start was to have been made at five o'clock in the morning and contrary to agreement but according to prophecy the Cantonment was left behind at just nine o'clock. The road leads past Joe Knutson's Spring creek ranch, across the Big Plateau, where Gifford Bros. and John Munro are putting up a thousand tons of hay. From here to Wadsworth's, the home ranch of the Bad Lands Cattle Co., the road leads over a country that no one but a Bad Lands pioneer would have thought of crossing except in a balloon. At Wadsworth's "the gang" stopped for dinner and the way the fresh milk and butter-milk was encircled would have astonished anyone not acquainted with Bad Lands apetites.

The gang upon starting, were warned that some of the river crossings were full of quicksand. One of them proved to be all the fondest fancy could paint it. Going down a steep pitch into the river, the double-tree began parting as soon as the quicksand was struck. "Pack." said Mack., "the measly pajimmicle's going to bust." Just then it did "bust," and Pack. who was driving, thought he would be jerked over the outer battlements of the Hence before he could get the team stopped. Then the team began sinking and Mack. sprang into the Little Muddy to lead them out. First the man was on top and then the horses. But Mack. "stayed with the leather" and got safe on shore with the horses, leaving the buck-board in the middle of the river. It must have been lots of fun but "the gang" have only just begun appreciating it. The muddy waters gurgled their enjoyment of the hilarity and the quicksand in its appreciation of the festivities opened its hospitable maw in a way that threatened a complete swallowing up of the outfit.

A double-tree was finally rigged with a couple of cottonwood saplings and some lariats, the horses were duly argued with and made to see the necessity of "getting a gait on 'em" and the bed of the Little Missouri began moving up with the buck-board. The shore was at last reached safely and a rest was made while "the gang" ate a quart each of choke-cherries, warranted to pucker boiler plate with one application.

About four o'clock Mack's ranch was reached, Pack. meantime stopping off and killing a supply of chickens. Then began the pleasure of a camping-out trip. The sensation of not having an earthly thing to do except to enjoy one's self was fully appreciated.

Mack. and Pack. arose at four the next morning and started after some chickens. A covey was soon flushed and bang! bang! bang! bang! Not a bird dropped. Mack. glared at Pack. and Pack. glowered at Mack. Another covey was flushed and another fusillade was started. Same result. More glaring. Again was a covey flushed and again did all the birds sail away unharmed.

"Guess you haven't lost any chickens" said Mack.

"Guess you haven't enough advantage over me to swear by" said Pack.

Then the latter got out a cartridge, lifted a wad and found a choice collection of rags and paper where the shot ought to have been.

"Mack, you're a gay deceiver" said Pack: "and I've got a mind to mow a ton of hay with you."

But Mack. was rolling on the ground fairly screaming with mirth. At last he held in long enough to say:

"Well I'll be jiggerdy jammed if I didn't put that job up on Fisher and when he [petered?] on the procession and didn't come, I forgot all about them."

Then ensued a great laying together of heads and the solemn promise of each to the other that they would never give the thing away. And neither ever will if the court knows herself.

Two shells loaded with shot were found and with one Pack. wounded a chicken and then ran it down and clubbed it to death, while Mack. crawled up so close to a cotton-tail rabbit, that when the other went off it blew the rabbit's head clear over the outer battlements of the New Jerusalem as Mack. graphically expressed it.

Several plausible lies were concocted to tell the waiting wives, to account for the large number of shots and the small size of the game bag. But they somehow failed to hold water under the caustic remarks of the "t'othermost halves."

The next day was devoted to hunting specimens and a splendid collection of leaf impressions in rock was obtained.

On the following day an early start was made down the river. On the way a wild goose was killed and it was immediately agreed that when the gang returned to Medora the number should be raised to thirteen. In a calmer moment, however, and in spite of Mack's. cogent reasoning that no one would believe it anyway, the number was lowered to three. This number now stands on record and is quoted with authority.

At the side of the road, on a high plateau was found Tompkin's hay camp. As Tompkins expressed it, the assent was "a leetle sidlin'." Further comment than that, Mack. who was driving, dropped his whip and it fell out over the hind seat in the buck-board is unnecessary. This is not stated as a fact but Mack. thought it would be a good scheme to say it was. It might be well to add, as giving force to the statement that Mack. is considered perfectly truthful in all his statements, by strangers.

On the top of the plateau were found Mr. and Mrs. Tompkins camped very snugly in a tent. The plateau was cool and airy, bringing appetites that did full justice to the bountiful dinner spread by Mrs. Tompkins.

The next objective point was the Elkhorn ranch where a warm welcome was received at the hands of Messrs. Sewall & Dow and their wives. This ranch is probably the best one on the river, being 20x60 and built very substantially. It is situated in a beautiful grove of cottonwoods and will be made a hunting head-quarters by Theodore Roosevelt, the owner. Mrs. Sewall and Mrs. Dow are strangers to the Bad Lands, only having arrived lately, but they and their husbands fully understand the art of hospitality and "the gang" was made to feel at home immediately.

A pleasant drive back to Mack's. ranch in the evening was followed in the morning by an early start for town. A road through the buttes avoided the bad river crossings. This road leads through the heart of the Bad Lands Cattle Co's. range and showed as fine a looking lot of cattle as one can see anywhere. The calves especially were numerous and in fine condition. Arrived at Wadsworth's, Miss Birdie was found keeping house. Rich milk was handed around until the bottom of a gallon pail was reached. A fresh start was made, the next stop being at Joe Knutson's, where an ice-cold drink from his spring and a raw turnip each, rustled from his garden refreshed the travellers. They arrived home rather tired but with enlarged ideas of Bad Lands hospitality.
articles.summary: Humorous account of "Mack." and "Pack." and their wives camping down the Little Missouri, including a quicksand mishap and a visit to Roosevelt's Elkhorn ranch.

events.title: Montana stock association meets at Helena without Little Missouri delegates
events.summary: The Cow Boy faulted the Little Missouri Stockgrowers' association for not meeting to name authorized delegates before the Montana association's semi-annual meeting at Helena, beginning Aug. 25.
events.excerpt: the semi-annual meeting of the Montana association at Helena, which begins Aug. 25.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Joe Ferris stocks ammunition and nails
events.summary: Joe Ferris received a full line of powder, shot and rifle cartridges and added a stock of nails.
events.excerpt: Joe Ferris has received a full line of powder, shot and rifle cartridges

events.date_basis: "last Wednesday evening"; the most recent Wednesday (19 Aug) is impossible since the train had already reached New York after eight days, so probably Wed 12 Aug 1885
events.title: Record tea train passes through Medora
events.summary: A train-load of tea that passed through Medora reached New York from Tacoma in eight days and four hours, 3,378 miles, the fastest ocean-to-ocean freight run yet.
events.excerpt: reached New York in eight days and four hours from Tacoma

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt's new saddles and outfits arrive
events.summary: Two saddles and outfits arrived, one for Theodore Roosevelt's own use and one a present from him to Chimney Butte cowboy George Myers, with Maltese Cross and Elkhorn brands in gold on the spurs; they cost about $300 in Cheyenne.
events.excerpt: One was for Theodore Roosevelt's own use and the other was a present by him to George Myers, a Chimney Butte cowboy.

events.date_basis: "died Sunday night" before Thu 20 Aug 1885; funeral Monday 17 Aug
events.title: Infant Earl Garver dies
events.summary: Earl, infant son of J. D. Garver, died of cholera infantum; at the funeral Monday J. C. Fisher and T. W. Gordon spoke, and burial was on Cemetery butte.
events.excerpt: Earl, infant son of J. D. Garver, died Sunday night of cholera infantum

events.title: John Munro marries Anne Brophy
events.summary: John Munro and Anne Brophy were married at the Catholic church by Father Martin of Mandan, with a wedding lunch at the Northern Pacific; the couple left for Miles City on a bridal tour.
events.excerpt: John Munro and Anne Brophy were married yesterday morning at the Catholic church, by Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Marquise de Mores' bear hunt reported by Vic Smith
events.summary: A letter from Vic Smith at Billings said the Marquise de Mores killed several bears on a mountain hunt (six bears for the party, plus a silver-tip by William VanDriesche); Smith called her "an excellent shot and fearless as a cowboy."
events.excerpt: Vic characterizes the Marquise as "an excellent shot and fearless as a cowboy."

events.title: John Winterling ships 700 cattle from Mingusville
events.summary: John Winterling is shipping 700 head of cattle from Mingusville.
events.excerpt: John Winterling is to-day shipping 700 head of cattle from Mingusville.

events.title: Stoddard & Howard ship 1,200 cattle from Dickinson
events.summary: Stoddard & Howard shipped 1,200 head of cattle from Dickinson.
events.excerpt: Stoddard & Howard shipped 1,200 head of cattle from Dickinson last Monday.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 20 Aug 1885; Buster returned "yesterday" (19 Aug)
events.title: Five hundred Hashknife cattle delivered
events.summary: J. W. Buster superintended the delivery of 500 Hashknife cattle to the company and returned to the Hashknife camp.
events.excerpt: superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle to the Co. last Saturday.

events.title: Ferris & Merrifield ship cattle from Chimney Butte ranch
events.summary: Ferris & Merrifield were to ship five car loads of cattle from the Chimney Butte ranch and Gregor Lang five cars from the Neimmela ranch, loaded at Dickinson.
events.excerpt: Ferris & Merrifield will ship five car loads of cattle from the Chimney Butte ranch to-day.

events.title: Thirteen stock cars burn at Mingusville
events.summary: Thirteen stock cars caught fire from a prairie fire and burned at Mingusville; the paper urged the railroad to build fire-guards.
events.excerpt: Thirteen stock cars were burned at Mingusville, Tuesday, catching from a prairie fire.

events.date_basis: letter received "last week" before Thu 20 Aug 1885
events.title: Cattle deaths at Sentinel Butte attributed to dry murrain
events.summary: H. Gilbert of Sentinel Butte wrote Ferris & Merrifield that a number of his cattle had died, apparently of dry murrain; no epidemic was feared.
events.excerpt: stating that a number of his cattle had died.

events.title: Three horses stray from the VI ranch
events.summary: Howard Eaton advertised for three sorrel horses branded VI that strayed from the VI ranch, last seen near the "Capital B" ranch.
events.excerpt: From the VI ranch on or about July 4, three sorrel horses branded VI on left hip.

events.date_basis: stated "in this issue" of Thu 20 Aug 1885
events.title: J. A. VanEeghen's horse brand first advertised
events.summary: J. A. VanEeghen's Garner Creek horse brand appeared for the first time; he planned ranch improvements to enlarge his band next spring.
events.excerpt: J. A. VanEeghen's horse brand appears for the first time in this issue of the Cow Boy.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Gordon opens branch clothing store at Medora
events.summary: An advertisement announced a new branch clothing, boot and shoe store at Medora under manager Thomas W. Gordon.
events.excerpt: New Store! (branch store at Medora), Thomas W. Gordon, Manager

events.title: Morton county sheriff visits Medora
events.summary: Geo. Harmon, sheriff of Morton county, visited Medora again.
events.excerpt: Geo. Harmon, sheriff of Morton county. was again a visitor to Medora last evening.

events.title: John Beers returns from the Hills with visitors
events.summary: John Beers returned from the Hills with Geo. Wilder and wife of Mt. Pleasant, Iowa.
events.excerpt: John Beers returned last Friday from the Hills, with Geo. Wilder and wife, of Mt. Pleasant, Iowa.

events.title: W. H. Minty returns from Wisconsin
events.summary: W. H. Minty returned alone from a visit to Augusta, Wis.
events.excerpt: W. H. Minty returned last Friday from his visit to Augusta, Wis.

events.title: McKee party leaves for Yellowstone
events.summary: The McKee party, with Mrs. and Miss Eaton, started for the National park.
events.excerpt: The McKee party, accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Eaton, started for the National park last Saturday evening.

events.title: N. G. Dakin calls while the editor is away
events.summary: N. G. Dakin, a boyhood friend of editor Packard, called while the editor was away.
events.excerpt: N. G. Dakin, an old boy-hood friend of the editor, called on us during our absence last week.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Wild plums abundant
events.summary: Wild plums were very abundant, and housewives were advised to preserve them.
events.excerpt: Wild plums are very abundant this year

events.title: Bob Roberts' sister arrives from Wales via Bismarck
events.summary: The sister of Bob Roberts, who came with him from Wales, arrived from Bismarck and is staying with Mrs. Paddock.
events.excerpt: arrived here from Bismarck last week and is now a guest of Mrs. Paddock.

events.title: Marquis de Mores orders a Medora man to get rid of his hogs
events.summary: A letter-writer said that in the spring the Marquis told a man keeping hogs in town to kill or sell them, and the man sold at a sacrifice.
events.excerpt: The Marquis went to him and told him he must either kill or sell them.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Citizen complains of slaughter-house offal and standing water
events.summary: "A Citizen" asked what had become of the Board of Health, complaining of uncovered offal from the slaughter-house and standing water between the hotel and saloon breeding malaria.
events.excerpt: what has become of our Board of Health?

events.date_basis: editor absent "last week"; party "just returned"; multi-day trip before Thu 20 Aug 1885
events.title: Packard party camps down the Little Missouri
events.summary: "Mack." and "Pack." and their wives made a camping trip, nearly losing their buck-board in quicksand at a Little Missouri crossing, hunting chickens, and visiting the Bad Lands Cattle Co. ranch, Tompkins' hay camp and Joe Knutson's.
events.excerpt: the double-tree began parting as soon as the quicksand was struck.

events.date_basis: during the excursion just returned from; before Thu 20 Aug 1885
events.title: Elkhorn ranch visited; Sewall and Dow wives newly arrived
events.summary: The excursion party was welcomed at the Elkhorn ranch by Sewall and Dow and their wives, who had only lately arrived. The house was described as 20x60 and well built, in a cottonwood grove, to be a hunting headquarters for owner Theodore Roosevelt.
events.excerpt: will be made a hunting head-quarters by Theodore Roosevelt, the owner.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 20 Aug 1885 issue
events.title: Gifford Bros. and John Munro put up hay on the Big Plateau
events.summary: On the Big Plateau, Gifford Bros. and John Munro were putting up a thousand tons of hay.
events.excerpt: Gifford Bros. and John Munro are putting up a thousand tons of hay.

events.date_basis: weather record for week; coldest Aug. 13, warmest Aug. 19
events.title: Hot week peaks at 99 degrees
events.summary: The Cow Boy observatory recorded noon temperatures up to 99 degrees on Aug. 19; Aug. 13 was the coldest day; prevailing wind northwest.
events.excerpt: Coldest day....Aug. 13. | Warmest day.Aug. 19.
